Three storefronts vs three language rows

App Store Connect splits two concepts indie teams often merge:

  • Storefront availability — which countries can download your app (Pricing and Availability). China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong are three separate checkboxes.
  • Localization rows — which language fields Apple indexes for each storefront. Greater China needs at least two rows, not one.

Typical mapping for Western indie apps shipping to all three:

  • China storefront → fill Chinese (Simplified, zh-Hans) — mainland script, mainland search terms (软件, 视频, 账号)
  • Taiwan storefront → fill Chinese (Traditional, zh-Hant) — Taiwan vocabulary (軟體, 影片, 帳號, 程式)
  • Hong Kong storefront → same zh-Hant row as Taiwan today, but buyer expectations skew toward English brand names in the title and Traditional copy in subtitle, description, and IAP labels

There is no “Hong Kong only” Connect locale row — Hong Kong pulls zh-Hant (or falls back to en-US if empty). China never reads your zh-Hant row for Search indexing on the mainland storefront. Treat three territories, two script families, two indexed language rows as the minimum honest setup.

What actually differs — script, keywords, tone, trademarks

Script and vocabulary

Simplified and Traditional are not font choices. Character pairs change meaning density in the 30-character title and subtitle: 网络/網路, 信息/資訊, 默认/預設. A zh-Hans description pasted into zh-Hant — or run through OpenCC — still carries mainland phrasing that Taiwan and Hong Kong buyers read as imported.

Keywords and search vocabulary

Each Connect row has its own hidden keyword field (~100 characters). China Search indexes zh-Hans terms; Taiwan and Hong Kong Search index zh-Hant terms independently from en-US and zh-Hans. Users in Taipei type different nouns than users in Shanghai for the same app category. Hong Kong Search often mixes English product names with Traditional Chinese problem phrases — your keyword row should reflect that mix without duplicating visible title text.

Tone and buyer expectations

Mainland zh-Hans listings can carry denser feature stacks; Taiwan zh-Hant buyers respond to concise outcome-first openings similar to good en-US copy. Hong Kong product pages frequently show an English app name with Traditional subtitle and description — not because Apple requires it, but because local skimming habits tolerate English brands when body copy is native Traditional. One tone setting does not fit three storefronts.

Trademarks and competitor names

Keyword fields in any Chinese row are not free-text ad slots. Do not paste competitor app names, celebrity names, or Apple trademark strings into zh-Hans or zh-Hant keywords to “borrow” search traffic — review rejection and competitor complaints apply across all three territories. AppLocale keeps trademark-safe phrasing; we do not pack competitor brands into your keyword rows.

FAQ

Are China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong one Chinese localization in App Store Connect?

No. Storefront availability is separate from language rows. Mainland China uses Chinese (Simplified, zh-Hans). Taiwan and Hong Kong use Chinese (Traditional, zh-Hant) — one shared Connect row for both territories, but different from zh-Hans. Hong Kong buyers often expect English product names with Traditional body copy. You need at least two language rows, not one paste.

Can I paste my Simplified Chinese listing into the Traditional Chinese row?

Character conversion (OpenCC) does not produce Taiwan or Hong Kong search vocabulary, payment terms, or ASO keyword habits. A zh-Hans row indexed for China reads mainland on a Taiwan or Hong Kong product page. zh-Hant is a separate Connect locale with its own title, subtitle, keywords, and description fields.

Paste-ready Simplified Chinese (zh-Hans) fields for the China storefront — title, subtitle, keywords, description, and keyword notes with rationale. If you specify both scripts at checkout, we can include Traditional Chinese (zh-Hant) alignment notes for Taiwan and Hong Kong. Delivered to the email on your Stripe receipt within 24 hours.
